quizName: DMV Practice Test #15 25 Questions • Passing Score 21

questions.question: During the day, your headlight should:

options.text: Switch between high and low beam.

questions.explanation: High beam headlights during the day help other drivers see you better. Use high beam anytime you are not directly behind or heading toward another vehicle.

questions.question: When riding in a group, inexperienced riders should be positioned:

options.text: At the back of the group.

questions.explanation: Less experienced riders should ride near the front, right behind the leader. This allows experienced riders behind them to watch over them.

questions.question: How does the stopping distance for motorcycles compare to cars?

options.text: Cars need much longer to stop.
Cars need a little longer to stop.
Both take about the same time to stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: Both take about the same time to stop.
questions.explanation: Under normal conditions, motorcycles and cars stop in almost the same distance. However, wet roads make it much harder for motorcycles to stop quickly.

questions.question: When going through a curve, you should:

options.text: Stay in the same part of the lane the entire time.
Always stay in the left part of the lane.
Always stay in the right part of the lane.
Remember that the best path may not follow the road curve.

questions.correctAnswerText: Remember that the best path may not follow the road curve.
questions.explanation: Road and traffic can change at any time. Be ready to move your lane position as needed. The best path through a curve may not match the curve of the road.

questions.question: Your lane position should do all of the following, except:

options.text: Help you see and be seen.
Keep you out of other drivers' blind spots.

questions.explanation: A good lane position helps you see others and be seen. It keeps you away from wind blasts, blind spots, and hazards. Your position should give other drivers less reason to share your lane and keep an escape route open if danger appears.

questions.question: The center of a lane often has an oily strip. This strip:

options.text: Is safe for motorcyclists unless it is raining.
Should always be avoided because other lane areas are safer.
Improves traction for most motorcycle tires.

questions.correctAnswerText: Is safe for motorcyclists unless it is raining.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in a strip down the center of the lane. When the road is dry, this area usually has enough grip for safe riding. The strip is only about two feet wide, so you can ride to one side of it and still be in the center of the lane.

questions.question: When being passed, do not move to the far side of your lane because:

options.text: The passing vehicle may move back into your lane too soon.
You may stop other vehicles from passing you.
The part of the lane near the passing vehicle is better.
You will feel more wind blast on the far side of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: The passing vehicle may move back into your lane too soon.
questions.explanation: When being passed, do not ride on the far side of your lane. This may encourage the other driver to move back into your lane before it is safe to do so.

questions.question: If it starts to rain while you are riding, you should:

options.text: Ride down the center of the lane.
Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: The center of a lane has oil deposits and becomes slippery when wet. When rain starts, ride in the tire tracks left by cars. Slow down on wet surfaces.

questions.question: A rider wearing a helmet is _______ more likely to survive a crash than a rider without one.
questions.explanation: Riders without helmets are three times more likely to die from head injuries than riders wearing helmets, no matter what speed they are traveling.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a common cause of motorcycle wobble?
questions.explanation: Most wobbles come from improper loading, wrong accessories, or incorrect tire pressure. Do not try to speed up to get out of a wobble.

questions.question: The best way to brake in a straight line is to:

options.text: Use the rear brake while downshifting.

questions.explanation: Use both the front and rear brakes together without locking either wheel. Always use both brakes when you slow down or stop.

questions.question: Swerving a motorcycle:

options.text: Should be done to avoid a hazard on a slippery road.

questions.explanation: Swerving is a quick move that needs a lot of grip on the road. Do not swerve on wet or slippery surfaces.

questions.question: When looking through a turn, you should:
questions.explanation: Look ahead through the turn to see where you want to go. Turn only your head, not your shoulders. Keep your eyes level.

questions.question: If your front tire locks while braking, you should:

options.text: Keep the brake engaged until you stop.
Release both brakes and coast to a stop.
Release the front brake and use only the rear brake.
Release the brake lever until the tire grips the road again.

questions.correctAnswerText: Release the brake lever until the tire grips the road again.
questions.explanation: If your front wheel locks, release the brake lever so the tire can grip the road again. Then apply the brake again.

questions.question: To swerve correctly:

options.text: Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.
Press the handgrip in the opposite direction of your turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.
questions.explanation: Press the handgrip on the side you want to turn. Press the opposite handgrip to return to your original direction once you clear the hazard.

questions.question: When stopping behind a vehicle, you should:

options.text: Stop far behind, then slowly move up.
Make a quick stop right behind the vehicle.
Stay about four car lengths behind.

questions.explanation: Stay well behind the vehicle in front of you. The vehicle could back up without warning, or another vehicle may come up from behind you.

questions.question: When entering a turn, a rider should:

options.text: Move their shoulders to match the turn angle.
Sit up as high as possible.

questions.explanation: Before entering a turn, reduce your speed by releasing the throttle and using both brakes if needed.

questions.question: With a three-wheeled motorcycle or sidecar, do not ride too far to the right because:

options.text: Other drivers may not see you.
You will have trouble passing other vehicles.
Other drivers may try to share your lane.
You may run off the road.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may run off the road.
questions.explanation: A sidecar sits on the right side. Riding too far right puts the sidecar at risk of leaving the road. On a three-wheeled motorcycle, the rear right wheel may also leave the road if you get too close to the right edge.

questions.question: Which formation is best for a group of riders on a curve?
questions.explanation: A staggered formation works well for most group riding. Use a single-file formation when turning, entering a curve, or getting on or off a highway.

questions.question: On a slippery surface, you should not:

options.text: Use only the front brake when slowing or stopping.
Use both brakes when slowing or stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use only the front brake when slowing or stopping.
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, reduce your speed, avoid sudden moves, and use both brakes. Watch for oil, dirt, gravel, shaded areas, and bridges, as these are more likely to be slippery.

questions.question: When riding a three-wheeled motorcycle through a curve, what should you do?

options.text: Stay in the center of the lane.
Stay on the outside of the lane.

questions.explanation: Three-wheeled motorcycles and motorcycles with sidecars turn differently than two-wheeled motorcycles. The best path through a curve may not follow the curve exactly. You may need to move from the outside of the curve to the inside before straightening out.

questions.question: When should you flash your brake light?

options.text: There is a stop sign ahead.

questions.explanation: Flash your brake light before slowing down if someone is following you too closely. The other driver may not see the hazard ahead that is causing you to slow down. Also flash your brake light if you are about to slow down where other drivers might not expect it.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of riding in a close group?

options.text: It takes up minimal space on the highway.
The group is easy to see.
The group is unlikely to be split up.
The riders will get to their destination more quickly in a close group than in a spread out group.

questions.correctAnswerText: The riders will get to their destination more quickly in a close group than in a spread out group.
questions.explanation: Riding in a close group is better than riding spread out because the group takes up less road space, is easier for others to see, and is less likely to be separated at traffic lights or during passes.

questions.question: When an operator's left arm is bent at the elbow and pointing upward, what does it mean?
questions.explanation: Operators use hand signals instead of mechanical turn signals. When the left arm is bent at the elbow and pointing upward, it means the operator plans to turn right or change lanes to the right.

questions.question: Why should you not change gears on railroad tracks?

options.text: Other drivers may not be expecting you to change gears.
The uneven surface may make it more difficult to switch gears.

questions.explanation: Do not shift gears when crossing railroad tracks. Your motorcycle might stall while on the tracks.
